## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kaḷāyamuṭṭhijātaka* (Ja 176), translated in modern listings as *The Lost Pea*, is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. In V. Fausböll's edition of the Jātaka commentary, it constitutes the sixth story of its vagga [Fausböll 1879]. The opening verse begins with the phrase *Bālo vatāyaṃ dumasākhagocaro* ("A foolish monkey") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework (*nidāna*), the Buddha related this account while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a king of Kosala (*Kosalarājānam ārabbha*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The prose commentary explains that during the rainy season, unrest broke out on the king's border; after his stationed warriors fought two or three engagements without overpowering their foes, they sent word to the king, who subsequently set out in unseasonable weather past the vicinity of Jetavana [Fausböll 1879].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus identifies any early cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan corpora, nor does DharmaNexus report any significant internal Pali text reuse matches for this Jātaka [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral currently records four translations of the text in four languages [SuttaCentral].
